---
title: "This is why the EU–Canada alliance matters"
subtitle: |
  The most important thing about the proposed alliance is not what it is called. It is that Canada and Europe are choosing to define it themselves.
categories: [politics, Europe, Canada, European Union, geopolitics, 2026]
date: "2026-09-17"
---

A new political relationship is proposed. It does not yet exist in law. Its institutions have not been designed. Its terms have not been negotiated.

And apparently this is confusing.

That was one of the stranger reactions to Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal that Canada become the European Union’s first “associate member.” [CBC News](https://youtu.be/7uUi6Cx94JA?is=Lmuyd8QEXOTEYEFw) spent much of its coverage explaining that there is no such legal category, that Canada cannot become an ordinary EU member because it is not European, and that von der Leyen cannot simply impose a new arrangement on the Union’s 27 member states.

All true.

And almost spectacularly beside the point.

Of course associate membership does not already exist. **She was proposing to create it.**

This is how politics works. It is how treaties work. It is how institutions work. Political actors decide that existing arrangements are inadequate, state an objective, negotiate the details, construct a legal framework, and—if they can assemble the necessary coalition—turn it into law.

Europe did not wake up after the Second World War to discover the European Coal and Steel Community conveniently waiting in a treaty book.

Robert Schuman first proposed something new. Governments then negotiated it. A treaty followed. Institutions followed the treaty. The European project itself is built on repeated acts of political imagination preceding the legal structures that eventually made them real.

The [Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950](https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/history-eu/1945-59/schuman-declaration-may-1950_en) explicitly anticipated that sequence: the political principles came first; a treaty and negotiated implementation would follow.

So the interesting question raised by von der Leyen’s proposal is not: **Where is “associate membership” in the current rulebook?**

It is: **What are Canada and Europe trying to build, and can they muster the political will to build it?**

That distinction matters because this proposal is about much more than an institutional label.

Von der Leyen used her [2026 State of the Union address](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RfYjukF1Pe8) to argue that Europe must become more capable of acting on its own behalf in an increasingly dangerous world. The Commission itself describes the State of the Union as the annual speech in which its president sets out priorities and ideas for shaping the Union’s future. In the [official transcript](https://cyprus.representation.ec.europa.eu/news/2026-state-union-address-president-von-der-leyen-2026-09-16_en), von der Leyen spoke about democratic states choosing their partners, reducing strategic dependencies, and deepening cooperation with Canada in defence, technology, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, quantum technology, cybersecurity and the Arctic.

Then she proposed taking the relationship to the “highest level possible” and opening the door to Canada as the EU’s first associate member.

[The European Parliament stood and applauded.](https://www.reuters.com/world/eu-opens-door-canada-become-first-associate-member-eu-commission-president-says-2026-09-16/)

That did not ratify a treaty. Nobody serious thinks it did.

But the idea that it was therefore “just symbolic” manages to misunderstand both symbolism and politics at once.

A parliament standing behind an unprecedented proposal tells us something. It tells governments something. It tells Canada something. It tells other countries something.

Political symbolism is not what remains after the “real” politics has been removed. Sometimes symbolism is itself an act of politics.

And in this case, the symbolism was unusually clear:

**Europe and Canada are asserting their ability to choose one another.**

That should be an utterly mundane proposition. Instead, the responses have revealed how unfamiliar the idea has become.

Donald Trump provided the most blatant example.

Asked about the proposed relationship, he called it “laughable” and warned that if he considered it a hostile act, the United States could impose very serious tariffs on Europe or stop trading with it in certain areas. [The Associated Press reported the threat directly](https://apnews.com/article/4078e9549ff9caa5ded08f7dd2f99065).

Think about what that means.

Canada and Europe consider changing the relationship between themselves, and the president of a third country immediately raises the possibility of economic punishment depending on whether he approves of their intentions.

There could hardly be a more concise demonstration of the strategic problem that “autonomy” is supposed to address.

If dependence on a powerful partner creates vulnerability to political pressure, then threatening countries because they attempt to reduce that dependence does not weaken the argument for diversification.

It illustrates it.

Dependence creates vulnerability. Vulnerability encourages diversification. Diversification produces threats. The threats demonstrate the value of diversification.

But the Canadian media reaction was revealing in a different way.

CBC’s chief political correspondent described the announcement as “confusing” and said von der Leyen’s declaration had “thrown a lot of us off guard.”

This is particularly strange because the basic idea was already public. On September 13, [Reuters reported](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/carney-pushes-idea-making-canada-associate-member-eu-wsj-reports-2026-09-13/) that Mark Carney had explicitly ruled out ordinary EU membership while saying Canada would begin discussions for a “unique alliance” with the Union. That report followed [The Wall Street Journal’s account](https://www.wsj.com/economy/canada-seeks-eu-associate-member-status-as-u-s-trade-talks-collapse-4eebec65) that an unprecedented form of associate status was being explored.

The next day, reporting citing a senior Canadian official said that “associate member” was one of several labels under consideration and that Canada was more interested in the substance of deeper ties than in what the relationship would be called. In other words, the distinction was already available: Canada was not seeking ordinary membership; Canada and Europe were discussing an unprecedented deeper relationship.

Those are not contradictory statements.

Canada can decline to become a conventional member of an existing institution while negotiating an unprecedented new relationship with it.

Yet much of the CBC discussion seemed trapped inside the existing categories. There is only one kind of membership. Canada cannot have that kind. The proposed alternative does not currently exist. Therefore the whole thing is murky, perhaps merely symbolic, perhaps not terribly realistic.

It is politics interpreted as taxonomy.

And the most charitable explanation may be the most interesting one: the idea had been reported, but nobody really believed it.

It was treated as speculation precisely because it did not fit comfortably within the existing map of the world.

Then von der Leyen stood before the European Parliament and made it a political proposal.

The failure was not necessarily one of information. It may have been a failure of imagination.

For decades, the international position of Canada and Europe has been extraordinarily stable.

Canada has been deeply economically integrated with the United States. European security has rested heavily on American military power. American technology companies dominate much of the digital infrastructure on which both depend. Washington has been so central to the Western political system that its centrality can begin to look less like an arrangement of power and more like a feature of reality.

Under those circumstances, European “strategic autonomy” can sound like rhetoric right up until Europe starts exercising it.

Canadian diversification can sound like branding right up until Canada begins constructing relationships that reduce its reliance on the United States.

And a novel Canada–Europe alliance can sound implausible right up until their political leaders stand together and announce that they intend to build one.

This is why the standing ovation mattered.

It did not tell us what France will demand in negotiations. It did not tell us what Poland will think about defence provisions, what agricultural concessions will survive, how regulatory alignment might work, whether mobility rights will be included, or what Hungary may decide to obstruct on any given Tuesday.

There will be disagreements.

There should be disagreements.

Twenty-seven democratic states do not suddenly acquire one opinion because Ursula von der Leyen gives a good speech.

Europe’s cumbersome system of distributed authority is one reason it can be maddeningly slow and strategically ineffective. The Commission proposes. Governments negotiate. Parliament participates. National interests collide. Lawyers descend. Years pass.

But that makes agenda-setting more important, not less.

Von der Leyen was not pretending to be an American president issuing an executive order. She was doing what political leadership in this system requires: stating where she believes Europe should go and attempting to build the coalition that can take it there.

The ovation showed that, at least in that chamber and at that moment, the idea resonated.

That is political information.

And perhaps the most important information is contained in the very bewilderment surrounding it.

The proposal seems radical partly because Canada and Europe have spent so long operating within an international architecture in which their independent strategic agency was constrained, delegated or simply taken for granted.

Now they are talking openly about changing that.

Carney had already framed the underlying objective explicitly. In remarks on September 15, he said Canada was deepening ties with trusted partners in order to increase its [“strategic autonomy”](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/speeches/2026/09/15/prime-minister-carney-delivers-opening-remarks-canada-investment-summit), because “integration has been weaponised” and arrangements work when partners respect one another’s sovereignty.

Nobody knows what “associate membership” will ultimately mean. The phrase may survive negotiations. It may be watered down. It may disappear entirely and leave behind a collection of agreements with a different name.

That is almost secondary.

After Carney met von der Leyen in Strasbourg, the Canadian government described the emerging arrangement as a move beyond CETA toward a “far stronger, more ambitious alliance” across defence, AI and compute, energy, space, critical minerals, financial infrastructure and digital trade. Most importantly, Ottawa described it as [“a unique approach that they will define together”](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/readouts/2026/09/16/prime-minister-carney-meets-president-european-commission-ursula-von-der).

That last phrase answers much of the confusion.

What exactly is associate membership?

They have not defined it yet.

Where precisely does it sit in the current treaties?

It does not. [Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/teu_2012/art_49/oj/eng) governs ordinary accession by a European state. But EU law also already allows the Union to conclude [association agreements with third countries](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2012/art_217/oj/eng). What this new relationship ultimately requires will depend on what Canada and Europe decide they want it to contain.

Who decides what it becomes?

Canada and Europe intend to negotiate that.

The uncertainty is not evidence that nothing is happening. **The uncertainty is the thing that is happening.**

And then came Trump’s reaction.

There is an almost perfect irony in threatening economic retaliation against countries because they are trying to reduce their vulnerability to economic coercion. If Canada and Europe are concerned that excessive dependence on any one partner limits their freedom of action, warning them that choosing other partners may provoke punishment does not undermine that concern. It illustrates it.

None of this guarantees that the emerging Canada–EU project will succeed. It may become less ambitious during negotiations. National governments may block important elements. Economic realities may constrain both sides. The term “associate membership” itself could eventually disappear and be replaced by something more legally conventional.

But focusing exclusively on those possibilities misses what has already changed.

The political declaration has happened.

Europe’s leadership has publicly said that it wants a more independent Europe capable of choosing its partners. Canada has publicly said it wants greater strategic autonomy and a much deeper relationship with Europe. The president of the European Commission has proposed inventing a new category for that relationship. The Canadian prime minister welcomed the initiative. And Europe’s elected parliament responded by standing up.

For decades, Canada and Europe have inhabited a geopolitical system in which their relationships with the United States were so central that alternatives could easily be treated as peripheral, unrealistic or almost conceptually strange.

Perhaps that is why the proposal produced such disbelief.

And perhaps that disbelief is part of the reason the moment matters.

The most consequential statement von der Leyen made was not “associate membership.” It was the principle immediately surrounding it: democratic countries must be free to choose whom they work with.

Canada and Europe have now begun to act as though they believe that principle.

Whatever legal structure eventually emerges from the negotiations, **that assertion of agency is already real.**
